title: Effects of realistic office daylighting and electric lighting conditions on visual comfort, alertness and mood
research_question: Do different photometric variables influence visual perception, comfort, and subjective non-visual variables (mood, alertness, well-being) in windowless office rooms under realistic daylighting (DL) versus electric lighting (EL) conditions, and how do these variables change over time?

participants.description: 25 healthy young subjects (9 women, 16 men; age=23.5±2.3 years, mean±SD) from Lausanne, Switzerland, without medical, psychiatric, or sleep disorders, and not extreme chronotypes. They maintained a regular sleep-wake cycle and abstained from alcohol/caffeine on study days.
participants.recruitment: Recruited at the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology in Lausanne (Switzerland).

stimuli_or_exposures.description: A 7m x 5m test room with a large window front (window-to-wall ratio of 0.5) and anidolic daylighting (DL) systems on the southern facade. For DL, lower window blinds were closed to prevent direct outside view, and daylight entered via upper windows and the anidolic system. For EL, opaque curtains prevented all daylight, and eight 58W fluorescent tube luminaires (4000K) provided electric light. Subjects were seated facing a wall, with the window to their left.

findings.mechanism: Higher CCT (bluer light component) in the late afternoon, associated with greater daylight availability, can acutely improve mood.
Poorer color rendition (lower CRI) in the late afternoon may make glare more noticeable or irritating.

mechanisms: Integration of visual and non-visual perceptual networks in the brain.
Time of day-dependent changes in subjects' internal state (e.g., circadian rhythms, fatigue).
Modulations by photometric properties (illuminance, CCT, CRI).
Acute effects of blue light component on non-visual functions like mood.
Adaptation or contrast effects from prior light exposure history.
moderators: time (hourly bins from noon to 6 pm)
implementation_implications: Need to identify and optimise interior lighting conditions, with respect to both visual and non-visual functions.
Daylight availability can be an indicator of occupants' work satisfaction, influencing both visual and non-visual functions.
Lighting effects depend on the lighting environment, time of day, and photometric properties.
Future office lighting environments should consider how visual acceptance and glare sensation interact with circadian and wake-dependent variations.

limitations: The dynamic nature of the DL condition made it difficult to fully disentangle whether variations over time were due to changes in photometric variables or subjects' internal state (time of day-dependent changes).

Subjective glare ratings remained stable over the afternoon, suggesting that the decrease in visual acceptance cannot be solely explained by glare sensations, unless participants became more glare sensitive as they became less relaxed.

The exact causes and mechanisms for the decrease of visual acceptance over time need further elucidation, potentially involving other behavioral variables or variations in subjective alertness, mood, etc.
Further investigation is needed to determine if visual acceptance and glare sensation undergo other circadian and/or wake-dependent variations.

paper_metadata.crossref_title: Effects of realistic office daylighting and electric lighting conditions on visual comfort, alertness and mood
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: Lighting conditions in workplaces contribute to a variety of factors related to work satisfaction, productivity and well-being. We tested whether different photometric variables also influence visual perception and the comfort of the lighting, as well as subjective non-visual variables such as mood, alertness and well-being. Twenty-five young subjects spent two afternoons either under electric light or daylighting conditions (without view from the window). Subjects overall preferred the daylighting for visual acceptance and glare. Changes of photometric variables modulated changes in visual light perception, alertness and mood in the course of the afternoon. Finally, we found several associations of visual and non-visual functions, indicating a potential relationship of visual comfort with other circadian and wake-dependent functions in humans, which consequently could impact office lighting scenarios in the future.
